title: Ines and the Glasshouse
premise: Emrys Thackeray, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost the ability to taste after their mother's diagnosis, drifts through a life of borrowed opinions until an unrecorded song surfaces on late-night radio—a song only their family ever knew, written by the mother and played once, the night the eldest brother left. The broadcast forces Emrys home to the glasshouse conservatory where the family arranged its silences, loyalties, and half-truths around what happened that night. As their mother's memory dissolves, each sibling offers a different version of the past, and Emrys must decide whether protecting the family story is worth losing the truth—and the mother—entirely. In the end, Emrys plays the song back to her one last time, tells her the truth she cannot remember, and finally tastes something again: salt, grief, and the first honest meal in years.
about_author: C. M. Thornbury is the pen name of a former food writer who spent a decade reviewing restaurants before leaving the trade to write fiction about families and the meals they avoid sharing together. They live near a botanical garden and claim to have never successfully grown anything.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Emrys files another glowing review for food they cannot taste, describing flavors from memory like a forger copying signatures. At home they eat standing over the sink, a tenant in their own body. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: hollow competence masking quiet dread.

chapters.title: Static on the Late Show
chapters.summary: Driving home at 2 a.m., Emrys hears a radio host play an unrecorded song—their mother's lullaby, 'Glasshouse,' which was never written down or performed outside the family. The DJ says it came from a demo tape mailed anonymously. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: vertigo; the private world has leaked.

chapters.title: Three Siblings, Four Versions
chapters.summary: Emrys calls each sibling about the broadcast. Brother Aeron denies it exists; sister Nia claims she sent the tape as a tribute; youngest brother Idris hangs up mid-sentence. Their mother, Bronwen, still lives in the old house with its crumbling glasshouse. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: suspicion blooming into obligation.

chapters.title: Return to the Conservatory
chapters.summary: Emrys arrives home; Bronwen greets them warmly but calls them by their dead father's name twice. The glasshouse is overgrown, the piano inside swollen with damp. Nia arrives too, cheerful and evasive. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: tenderness laced with unease.

chapters.title: What Mother Remembers
chapters.summary: Bronwen recounts the night of the song vividly—but her version ends before the fight, before anyone left, as if a page were torn out. She hums 'Glasshouse' perfectly yet cannot say who wrote it. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: grief for a memory still technically alive.

chapters.title: Nia's Tribute
chapters.summary: Nia admits sending the tape but insists she recorded Bronwen humming years ago, legally hers to share. Her version of the past casts Aeron's departure as simple ambition. POV: Nia. Emotional beat: devotion that curdles into control.

chapters.title: Aeron's Ledger
chapters.summary: Aeron, a solicitor in Cardiff, meets Emrys and warns against 'excavating.' He reveals he left home at nineteen after a row he refuses to describe, and that Bronwen asked him never to return while the glasshouse stood. POV: Aeron. Emotional beat: guilt armored as pragmatism.

chapters.title: Idris in the Wings
chapters.summary: Idris, estranged longest, works stage crew at a local theatre. He tells Emrys the song wasn't just a lullaby—it was written for someone specific, and it wasn't any of the children. He won't say who. POV: Idris. Emotional beat: wounded loyalty, withheld truth.

chapters.title: The Taste Test
chapters.summary: At a roadside café, Emrys orders their childhood favorite, Welsh rarebit, and tastes nothing. A young waitress asks if the review will be kind; Emrys realizes they've been reviewing their own numbness for years. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: humiliation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Letters Under the Potting Bench
chapters.summary: Clearing the glasshouse, Emrys finds a tin of unsent letters in Bronwen's hand, addressed to a name none of the siblings know: 'Elen.' The earliest predates all four children. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: the thrill and terror of evidence.

chapters.title: Nia's Version, Revised
chapters.summary: Confronted with the letters, Nia admits she knew of Elen—Bronwen's sister, erased from family stories after a quarrel over the house. Nia argues some erasures are mercy. POV: Nia. Emotional beat: loyalty weaponized as love.

chapters.title: Aeron Breaks Ranks
chapters.summary: Aeron arrives unannounced, having learned about the letters, and confesses his departure followed a fight over selling the glasshouse to pay Elen's debts. Bronwen chose the building over the sister. POV: Aeron. Emotional beat: relief and shame arriving together.

chapters.title: Bronwen's Good Day
chapters.summary: On a lucid afternoon, Bronwen walks Emrys through the glasshouse naming every plant her sister gave her, then asks, plainly, 'Have you found Elen yet?' She knows more than her children assumed. POV: Bronwen. Emotional beat: devastating clarity inside fog.

chapters.title: The Search for Elen
chapters.summary: Emrys traces Elen to a care home two counties away, alive, sharp-tongued, and unwilling to speak until Emrys admits they can't taste anything—an honesty that unlocks hers. Elen begins the true story of the song. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: truth traded for truth.

chapters.title: Elen's Account
chapters.summary: Elen reveals 'Glasshouse' was written by Bronwen for Elen the night Elen left—not a lullaby for children at all. The family myth was built to keep the children from feeling exiled by their mother's grief. POV: Elen. Emotional beat: compassion for the architecture of lies.

chapters.title: The Tape's Second Voice
chapters.summary: Replaying Nia's tape, Emrys hears a second voice beneath Bronwen's humming—Elen's, harmonizing. Nia knew all along and edited the broadcast copy to hide it. Confrontation shatters the sibling truce. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: betrayal inside the sanctuary.

chapters.title: Fracture
chapters.summary: The siblings argue in the glasshouse as a storm cracks two panes; old accusations surface—money, favoritism, who stayed. Bronwen wanders in mid-fight and asks why everyone is shouting about a song she doesn't know. POV: rotating among siblings. Emotional beat: the family's founding wound reopened.

chapters.title: What Staying Cost
chapters.summary: Alone with Bronwen overnight during her worst confusion, Emrys keeps her calm by humming 'Glasshouse' wrong on purpose until she corrects him—her memory outlasting her facts. He understands: the song is the truest thing she owns. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: love without illusion.

chapters.title: The Question Arranged Around
chapters.summary: Emrys gathers the siblings and poses the question the family was built to avoid: did Bronwen choose the glasshouse over Elen, or did the children need her to? Each must answer aloud. Aeron weeps; Nia goes silent; Idris laughs, finally free. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: climax—truth demanded at last.

chapters.title: Bringing Elen Home
chapters.summary: Against Nia's protest, Emrys drives Elen to the glasshouse. The sisters meet; Bronwen, deep in forgetting, recognizes not the name but the harmony, and joins Elen singing 'Glasshouse' complete for the first time in fifty years. POV: Emrys observing. Emotional beat: reconciliation beyond memory.

chapters.title: The Last Review
chapters.summary: Bronwen declines quickly now, peaceful, surrounded by all four children and Elen. After the funeral, Emrys writes a final review—not of a restaurant but of the glasshouse, published under their own name, resigning from criticism. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: release.

chapters.title: Salt
chapters.summary: Months later, Emrys cooks rarebit in the restored glasshouse for the scattered, mended family. The first bite tastes of cheese, mustard, and salt—tears, probably. Some things return when you stop performing them. POV: Emrys. Emotional beat: quiet, earned belonging.
